en: The Ritual Text for Maintaining the Fast, Reciting the Buddha’s Name, Repentance, and Prostration; Regarding the Names of Buddhas, one fears that [due to] such and such [obstacles],
one will be oppressed and have no leisure or respite, and one's transgressions will reach their utmost limit.

For hundreds and thousands of kalpas, there is no time of liberation, nor is there any leisure. Even though one may worship and make offerings to the Buddhas, if one is stingy and begrudges the merit [of others], it is therefore briefly set forth here.

In the twelfth month, according to the *Lidai Fabao Ji* (Record of the Dharma Treasures of Successive Dynasties) and other sources: On the first day of the first month, at dawn, one should face south and perform four prostrations to eliminate the sins of one hundred kalpas.
On the ninth day of the second month, at the hour of cockcrow, one should face north and perform four prostrations to eliminate the sins of one hundred kalpas.
On the seventh day of the third month, at the hour of the setting sun, one should face west and perform four prostrations to eliminate the sins of three hundred kalpas.
At midnight on the eighth day of the fourth month, one should perform four prostrations facing north to eliminate the sins of one hundred and thirty kalpas.
At dusk on the sixth day of the fifth month, one should perform four prostrations facing south to eliminate the sins of four hundred kalpas.
At dusk on the third day of the sixth month, one should perform six prostrations toward the east to eliminate the sins of five hundred kalpas.
At noon on the sixth day of the seventh month, one should perform nine prostrations toward the east to eliminate the sins of six hundred and twenty thousand kalpas.
On the eighth day of the eighth month at noon, facing south, perform nine prostrations to eliminate three hundred and twenty thousand kalpas of offenses.
On the ninth day of the ninth month at noon, facing east, perform nine prostrations to eliminate three hundred and thirty thousand kalpas of offenses.
On the seventh day of the tenth month at dusk, one should prostrate toward the south to eliminate the offenses of four thousand kalpas.
On the thirteenth day of the eleventh month at dusk, one should perform four prostrations toward the south to eliminate the offenses of four thousand kalpas.
On the thirteenth day of the twelfth month at dusk, one should face south and perform thirty prostrations to eliminate the sins of four *kalpas*.
At that time, the Tripitaka Master transcribed this list of Buddha names from the Imperial Decree and distributed it throughout the various provinces in this world of the five turbidities.
If there is a virtuous woman who can wholeheartedly receive and uphold this rite of homage—
relying upon the rite for sustaining kalpas—
her transgressions will be eliminated for as many incalculable kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
After the end of life, they will take rebirth [in a pure land], sitting upon a precious lotus flower and experiencing all manner of bliss.
At their thought, garments of fine silk and brocade appear in a thousand layers;
at their thought, food of a hundred flavors arrives in abundance.
Furthermore, those who can teach others to receive and uphold this rite shall unfailingly obtain the concentration that eliminates eighty-two thousand five hundred offenses.
Moreover, briefly stated, every month’s "evil days" are all the Ten Uposatha Days.

If you observe the fast and recite the Buddha’s name on this day, you will not follow [the path to] the Sword-Tree Hell; if you observe the fast and recite the Buddha’s name on the eighth day, you will not follow [the path to] the Iron Plow Hell; on the fourteenth day, the decree shall descend.
On this day, by observing the fast and reciting the Buddha’s name, one will not fall into the Hell of Boiling Cauldrons. On the fifteenth day, the Great Deity of the Five Paths descends;
on this day, by observing the fast and reciting the Buddha’s name, one will not fall into the Hell of Excrement. On the eighteenth day, King Yama descends.
On this day, by observing the fast and reciting the Buddha’s name, one will not fall into the Hell of Sawing. On the twenty-third day, the Great Heavenly General Tian descends;
on this day, by observing the fast and reciting the Buddha’s name, one will not fall into the Hell of the Copper Pillar. On the twenty-fourth day, Chameng descends.
On this day, by observing the fast and reciting the Buddha’s name, one will not fall into the Iron Bed Hell. On the twenty-eighth day, the Lord of Mount Tai descends;
on this day, by observing the fast and reciting the Buddha’s name, one will not fall into the Iron Fork Hell. On the twenty-ninth day, the Four Heavenly Kings descend.
On this day, by observing the fast and reciting the Buddha’s name, one shall not fall into the Hell of the Knife Mountains. On the thirtieth day, Śakra and Brahmā, the Heavenly Kings, descend;

on this day, by observing the fast and reciting the Buddha’s name, one shall not fall into the Iron Wheel Hell. The above ten days of fasting are all occasions when the sons and youths of the great deities, as well as the messengers who examine life spans, descend.
The note regarding the timing states:
"It descends immediately after the midday meal.
We respectfully request that the assembly exert every effort when the time arrives.
Recite the Buddha’s name and cultivate goodness with care, lest you be caught by the records of the karmic overseers and thus incur guilt and transgressions;
who then could save you?
It is simply because the True Teaching is vast and remote.
Without accumulating merit, one cannot reach [the shore];
the sea of suffering is difficult to ascend.
Without a boat or ship, one cannot cross it.
His mouth is like that of the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa;
through this holy transformation he has manifested his form. Beyond the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he stands as a Wheel-Turning King in the field of meritorious karma.
For this reason, Śākyamuni cultivated the Way, relying upon six years of arduous toil.
The youth sacrificed his own body to seek the eight characters of a four-line verse;
the ocean of the Buddha’s merit cannot be fully extolled.
Now, before this seat, the host of the vegetarian feast bows his head in homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma of Prajñā, and the noble Sangha of Arhats.
Immediately, Bei Fu appeared before him and requested that the assembly make a perpetual vow:
"May my family and dependents remain in peace; I respectfully prepare this single offering of vegetarian food and alms to provide for you.
I pray that from this day forward, the fragrant waters of Mount Gandhamādana may wash and cleanse our bodies and minds."
The supreme *amṛta* flows within his body;
his form is like a jeweled mountain, immovable and unshakable, as enduring as life itself.
Now, the mountain has shifted, yet his spirit abides eternally in the realm of the eternal.
Because her awakening advances daily, her wisdom-karma is lofty and brilliant, her merit is equal to that of a virtuous vow, and her life-span is like adamant;
thus, the woman freely possesses these excellent virtues, resembling the blossoming of a refined emerald tree.
Its exquisite beauty and graceful form resemble clusters of flowers shining with luster.
Furthermore, by virtue of this successive merit,
I pray that the sagely transformation of the Emperor and Empress shall be inexhaustible.

Sitting upright upon the Terrace of the August Emperor, he did not adhere to the transformations of the thousand kings; as the twilight of the era drew near, from the time of the Sage’s arrival until now, people from foreign lands have come in competition, clutching divine charts. Plowmen yield their ridges and travelers part ways on the road; the sagely mandate flourishes eternally, extending its bounty through ten thousand generations.
The three realms are transformed into a pure land; the hells become a city of fragrance.

All emerge from the gate of suffering and ascend the path of enlightenment. In a Brahma-voice, he asked: "How can one attain long life? How does the Buddha obtain an indestructible vajra-body? By what causes and conditions does he attain great, firm power? How, regarding this sutra, Can one ultimately reach the other shore? I pray that the Buddha will reveal its subtle mysteries And speak extensively for the sake of all sentient beings."

For the sake of the twenty-eight classes of devas, Śakra, Brahmā, and others, who pay homage to the eternally abiding Triple Gem; for the sake of the patrons, adorned with merit and wisdom, who pay homage to the eternally abiding Triple Gem; and for the sake of the sentient beings of the six realms so that they may be freed from obstacles and attain liberation, I prostrate to all worthy and holy ones. [I offer] this food and recite these prayers of aspiration.
Now, the food offered as this alms is presented to the Buddhas above,
offered to the worthy sages in the middle,
and extended downward to all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, so that they may all be equally satiated; thus one makes this offering of food.
The fragrant food has not yet been touched;
the upper portion is offered to the Buddhas,
and the middle portion is presented to the worthy sages.

May it extend downward to all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, so that they may all be universally satiated. [The officiant] recites the incantation for the food and makes this vow: "I respectfully address the Great Assembly.

Whatever deficiencies there may be in the vegetarian meal prepared by this disciple, which was collectively prepared by our hands yet does not accord with the Dharma, I pray that the Assembly will accept it."
With great compassion and joyful generosity,
he addressed the great assembly once more:
"The meal for the assembly has been prepared by your disciple."

It is permitted for the hands to work together to prepare many things that are not in accordance with the Dharma. When there is leftover food remaining from the midday meal, it is permitted for the assembly to dispose of the surplus by distributing it to those at the place where the Universal Recitation is held.
The world is like empty space;
like a lotus flower, it is unsullied by water.
Your mind is pure and transcends that [world]. I prostrate to the Unsurpassed Honored One who bestows blessings through his incantations and prayers.
Since both [the recipient and the donor] are the foremost of all practices in relinquishing attachment and abandoning stinginess and greed,
the donor now fears that the fruit of this completed vegetarian feast may not be complete;
therefore, he further offers pure wealth as an act of giving.
May those who have passed away be reborn in the Western Land;
may those currently living see their nature and realize the Buddha-way. With all reverence, we take refuge in the Buddha.
May all beings embody and understand perfect enlightenment and resolve to attain Bodhicitta. We take refuge in the Dharma.
When taking refuge in the Saṃgha, one should wish: "May all sentient beings enter deeply into the treasury of the sūtras, their wisdom as vast as the ocean;
may they govern the great assemblies with total unimpededness, harmonizing both men and women among the listeners."

All recite together: The wondrous form-body of the Tathāgata is peerless in the world; it is incomparable and inconceivable. Therefore, I now pay homage. The form of the Tathāgata is inexhaustible, and his wisdom is likewise so; all dharmas abide eternally. Therefore, I take refuge and pay homage to the eternally abiding Triple Gem. Bodhisattva Rājaprabha then spoke this *dhāraṇī* mantra: [Mantra follows]
Tiao dī dì tú sū tiē ā ruò mì dì míng dū tiē tiao qí tiē bō lài dì tiē yé mí ruò tiē míng dū tiē jù luó dì tiē qí mó tiē shā pó hē wáng nǚ jiē.
The seat of enlightenment dwells within the mind; One sits and reclines in the hall of nirvana.
The body itself is Amitābha Buddha—where else could one seek the Western Land? The Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara Dhāraṇī says:
This is called the Great Heart Mantra:
Oṃ āryāvalokiteśvara bodhisattva mahāsattva mahākāruṇika tadyathā oṃ arule svāhā. This mantra possesses great efficacy in subduing all diseases caused by spirits.
Furthermore, there are those who possess spirits and ghosts that undergo transformations,
manifesting as wild beasts, barbarians, or various other forms to enter into human bodies;
when one possesses such beings, one must strictly maintain ritual purity.
To cause all officials to rejoice, recite the mantra as follows:

Namo Tārā-devī-rakṣitā-devī, who can cause rulers and ministers to rejoice and not be angry. Svāhā. Namo Vāsuki-tārā. Namo Mahā-śūra-aṅgada. Namo Pradharṣa-mahādeva-mi-yūta. Namo Khadiravani-tā. Hūlu hūlu svāhā. The mantra for advancing toward the fruit, attaining realization, and cultivating practice is as follows:
Tathā-tathā-mūlura mūlura āpala mūlura-vigīkṣaya svāhā. If there are those who receive, uphold, read, and recite this, while simultaneously cultivating meritorious deeds.
This person is a Bodhisattva of the First Ground; I take refuge in Amitābha Buddha of the West.
The Buddha resides in the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the western direction;
I universally exhort all to be of one mind so that we may be born together in that place.
Regardless of noble or humble status, all are clearly guided;
it is only that ordinary beings fail to accomplish their practice.
First and foremost, one must never forget to recite the Buddha's name.
Second, one must ensure that mind and speech are in harmony.
Third, diligently cultivate the practice of the six perfections.
Fourth, do not seek fame and reputation outside of the fruits [of practice].
If one can thus accord with the Buddha’s intention,
then at the time of death, one shall go directly toward the lotus in that land facing east.
Following the Buddha through the six realms to save sentient beings, one will be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha of the Western Quarter.

The sentient beings of the six realms cannot be saved if, upon seeing the Buddha’s radiant light, they do not resolve their minds for enlightenment; though Amitābha calls them personally, they are unwilling to go.
The ox-headed jailers vied with one another to come and meet him as he approached his karmic retribution;
even though the Buddha himself came to rescue him, it was of no avail, for the boiling cauldrons and burning coals grew ever more intense. Upon hearing this, the Buddha asked:
"What sins has this person committed?"
Refrain from drinking alcohol, eating meat, and committing sexual misconduct;
I universally exhort all those in the place of practice to vow to cast off this body of pus and blood from Jambudvīpa.
I vow to be reborn together with all sentient beings in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Namo to Amitābha Buddha of the West.
Entering the True Gate once, never to turn back—thus, join the palms in reverence.
The mind sits upon the precious terrace;
the water of eight virtues is ever full.
Lotus flowers surround it on all four sides as they come toward the Buddha.
The Buddha emits light from the mark between his eyebrows to illuminate sentient beings of the lower realms;
the flowers open of their own accord as he intends to rescue them in other lands.
Amidst all sufferings, they dare to obtain two pearl robes upon their bodies.
I universally exhort all those in the place of practice:
with single-minded devotion, recite the Buddha’s name and enter the gateway of truth;
may you and all sentient beings together be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha of the Western Quarter.
Sitting alone upon a golden lotus, he manifests radiant light and the supreme path of ultimate gathering.
May all suffering sentient beings desire to return together to that one place.
One must be diligent and refined in practice until it is perfected;
the Bodhisattva internally cultivates the ten wholesome paths,
while the ordinary person externally pursues fame and reputation.
The Buddha-dharma is vast and inclusive, without duality;
yet fools differentiate it into various categories of practice.
Some say this body is of the same nature [as the Buddha].
Some say that the Buddha’s nature seeks names;
such people are not alone. They are surely destined for the pits of the three miserable realms and the six destinies.
May I sever dualistic views and cultivate equanimity;
may I be spontaneously born in the Pure Land of the West.
May I, together with all sentient beings, be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha of the Western Quarter.
You all should single-mindedly cultivate the practices for the Pure Land;
you must sit alone and contemplate with pure discernment.
Do not say that you shall go to Jambudvīpa;
in an instant, without ceasing, there is impermanence.
Life is like the flame of a lamp in the wind.
It is also like a flash of lightning amidst the clouds;
lacking protection from the three miserable realms and eighteen sufferings,
where can one hide when impermanence strikes all at once?
Suddenly reflecting on this, it is deeply lamentable:
how can one not be struck with alarm day and night?
Since antiquity, the sages and worthies have never ceased their efforts to avoid death.
How much more so for ordinary people who have attained long lives?
The practitioner exerts effort to cultivate the ten wholesome paths;
knowing that the body is not eternal, they realize it is impermanent.
I vow to be reborn together with all sentient beings in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha of the Western Quarter.
This disciple’s own nature dwells within the three realms.
In the long night of darkness, all is murky and dim;
wandering through the six realms of rebirth without rest,
one has never yet heard the sound of the Pure Land.
Having encountered a spiritual friend today,
I pray that I may cast off this foul and impure body of an ordinary person and obtain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Spontaneously born upon a lotus pedestal,
may I and all sentient beings together be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss. Namo Amitābha Buddha.
Now, observing this body,
it is truly loathsome—
a body of various impurities, merely a provisional designation.
Three hundred fragments of bone support one another;
in this leaking body, where has there ever been even a fragment of reality?
Lipstick and rouge merely adorn the consciousness.
In the end, they return to the underworld as dust;
their afflictions blaze fiercely without rest,
all of which are the causes for wandering through the three miserable realms.
I universally exhort all those in the place of practice:
exert yourselves with diligence to cultivate the causes for the Pure Land,
and vow together with all sentient beings to be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha of the Western Quarter.
Those who have entered the three miserable realms find it difficult to escape;
for kalpas they endure suffering bodies.
When the time of death arrives, one will naturally lack any wholesome roots;
the mind will be frantic with fear and filled with self-distrust,
as all karmic offenses and deeds will manifest before one's eyes.
The cauldron and furnace pass before one's eyes;
the ālayavijñāna undergoes all manner of suffering.
The four great elements are buried deep within the earth and hidden away.
Having now obtained a human body, if one does not contemplate the Buddha,
one will be reborn in a borderland as a hairless beast.
May all sentient beings be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha of the Western Quarter.
My previous existence as a beast with fur and horns was the cause of my present suffering and distress.
They commit the sin of killing without ceasing;
they treat their teachers and monks with contempt and act recklessly toward their parents;
they drink alcohol and eat meat without shame or remorse.
Today, to whom can one recount this suffering?
With the mouth obstructed, one cannot speak;
in various ways, the body is whipped by others.
With piercing pain, two tears fall from my eyes;
I universally exhort you to give rise to a virtuous mind for future lives,
and vow together with all sentient beings to be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha of the Western Quarter.
Throughout kalpas past, I have harbored illness and arrogance;
through ignorance, the three poisons have arisen.
When one realizes that one is constantly being befriended by the six thieves,
and when one returns to see that one has returned to the great earth.
Unaware, their natural minds were suddenly startled;
each with diligent hearts cultivated wholesome karma,
striving forward to avoid the pit of fire.
I vow to be reborn together in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha of the Western Quarter.
Contemplate with clarity that there is a land in the west.
In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha.
He dwells and preaches the Dharma for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
universally severing the various māras for the sake of the world.
Seated upon the throne of sainthood within the city of Anurādhapura,
he was surrounded by all the devas who came to visit him;
there were eighty-four thousand assemblies of bodhisattvas.
I offer flowers and fruits to purify this Sahā world.
May I, together with all sentient beings, be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Namo to Amitābha Buddha of the Western Quarter.
The celestial palaces all emerged from mid-air;
seven-jeweled towers and halls appeared, with *dhvaja*, *patākā*, canopies, and flowers filling the space, while golden branches and jade trees manifested spontaneously.
Agate and crystal form the great earth;
the great ocean is made of śarkara sand.
